title: Why Hindus bathe the Shiva linga
hookLine: Shiva drinks the world's poison, and devotees pour cool water over his linga
carry: abhisheka cools the one who drank the poison
tomorrow: The pillar of fire with no end

lines: A POISON THAT BURNS THE WORLDS.
cards: The gods and the demons are churning the ocean of milk, pulling a great serpent back and forth around a mountain, hoping to bring up the nectar of immortality.
Before any treasure, something else comes up: a poison so strong its fumes start to burn the worlds. Everyone runs. Everyone goes to Shiva.
And Shiva gathers the poison in his palm and drinks it. He holds it in his throat, where it stays, and his throat turns blue. That's why one of his names is Nilakantha, the blue-throated one.

teach.b: Now walk into a Shiva temple. Above the stone linga hangs a small pot with a pinhole in its base, and water drips onto the stone, one drop and then the next.

On festival days priests sit close and pour water and milk over the linga while they chant. The bath is called abhisheka, and when the Rudram is chanted with it, people call the rite Rudrabhisheka. Why bathe this god?
An old saying puts it simply: Vishnu loves to be adorned, Shiva loves to be bathed.

And many devotees tie it to the churning: the one who swallowed the world's poison, with fire in his third eye, is offered coolness, again and again. Hold the hymn next to the water and it makes the same movement.
It opens by bowing to Rudra's anger, his arrow and his bow, and asks that the bow be unstrung.

teach.h: TO THE KIND ONE, AND KINDER STILL.
teach.b: Deep inside comes the line namah shivaya cha shivataraya cha: a bow to the kind one, and to the one kinder still.
A traditional saying calls the Rudram the heart of the Vedas, namah shivaya the heart of the Rudram, and shi-va the heart of those five syllables. Take it as a picture, not a measurement.
That's the teaching of the bath: Shiva took in the world's poison so others wouldn't have to, and devotees answer with water and a bow, one drop at a time, until the fierce one shows his kind face.

how: In Shiva temples and in homes, Hindus may chant the Rudram during abhisheka, pouring water, milk and other offerings over the linga; some families arrange a Rudrabhisheka for a festival, a new home, or a hard time.

games.q: priests are chanting the Rudram while water pours over the linga. why water, for this god?
o: to wash the hymn's fierce opening away.
Shiva loves to be bathed: the one who drank the poison is offered coolness.
because water is the only offering the hymn allows.
games.why: an old saying: Vishnu loves to be adorned, Shiva loves to be bathed. many devotees add: he swallowed the world's poison, so he's offered coolness, one drop at a time.

practice: Bring to mind one thing that feels like poison right now, a worry, a hard word, a deadline with its bow drawn, and without fighting or fixing it, picture cool water poured slowly over it on each out-breath, the way the priests pour over the linga.
Let the thing stay what it is, and just keep pouring. If you pray, you can say namah shivaya softly with each pour, or the name of God you use; if you don't, let each out-breath be the pour.

wordCard.voice: The Rudram. A Vedic hymn that bows to the fierce Rudra until Shiva, the kind one, appears at its heart. Today, chanted as water pours over the linga of the blue-throated one.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Rudra, the Vedic name the hymn bows to, the fierce form of Shiva.
